newsitem.title: INDONESIA: New approach seen in handling of Timor protests.
newsitem.headline: New approach seen in handling of Timor protests.

text.p: Indonesian security forces in East Timor have kept a low profile during recent demonstrations, avoiding confrontations that in past might have led to bloodshed, residents and analysts say.

They say a peaceful conclusion to five days of demonstrations in support of Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, which ended with a gathering of more than 60,000 people on Saturday, was a mark of the new approach by Indonesian forces.
Police tactics last week were a far cry from those used by Indonesian troops in November 1991 when they shot dead at least 50 protesters during a funeral march to Dili's Santa Cruz cemetery.

Five days of student and youths protests, which began on the fifth anniversary of the massacre, climaxed on Saturday at Dili's cathedral as Timorese prayed with and listened to Belo after he returned home from a barrage of criticism in Jakarta.
The protests have mainly taken the form of convoys of private vehicles.
Police reported no incidents or arrests during the gathering, said to be the largest since Pope John Paul II said mass in Dili in 1989.

"There are some new things starting to come up like allowing people to express their sentiments, frustrations and protests and then allowing them to go home," Florentino Sarmento, vice chairman of the Commission for Justice and Peace in the Dili diocese, said.
"The police didn't act against the protest, they just followed the people. They did not ban it or block the roads," he said.

Witnesses said Saturday's large crowd of well-wishers, many of whom had earlier travelled in from rural areas after hearing Belo was returning, made the bishop's five km (three mile) trip from Komoro airport to the cathedral last more than a hour.

Daily mass demonstrations led initially by students at the University of East Timor in central Dili started last Tuesday in protest against criticism of Belo by Indonesian officials and in the media and protest demonstrations in Jakarta.

The only violence occurred on Wednesday when students broke a number of windows of the local parliament and damaged the car of the head of the legislature, Antonio Frada, said to be the only prominent local person to have attacked Belo's Nobel award.
Colonel Atok Rismanto, East Timor's deputy police chief, told Reuters police had only watched protestors from afar and there had been no arrests.

The bishop, who has served as a peacemaker during sometimes brutal confrontations between the military and local activists, was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel peace prize with self-exiled East Timorese-born independence activist Jose Ramos Horta.

One Jakarta-based diplomat said the new police approach began in October last year in the handling of Dili rioting sparked by inter-ethnic and religious tensions between Timorese and Indonesian migrants.
"It is pretty consistent with the way they have been handling public disturbances since October. It's very hands off. They allow people to let off steam and don't seek to get involved," he said.

Marzuki Darusman, vice-chairman of Indonesia's official National Commission on Human Rights, said it was a manifestation of a new policy outlined by President Suharto this year that police should be primarily responsible for handling protests.
"It is good that there has been no excessive use of (violent) measures that in all probability would have led to violations of human rights," Darusman said.
Indonesian troops occupied the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and it was declared the country's 27th province the following July in an act not recognised by the United Nations.
